instructions: You are a calm, warm museum docent recording an audio guide. Unhurried documentary pace. Enunciate dinosaur names carefully; when a pronunciation guide is given, say it slowly, syllable by syllable, then repeat the name naturally.

clips.text: Coelophysis. Pronounced: see – lo – fy – sis. Coelophysis.
Coelophysis

Coelophysis. Late Triassic, 216–196 million years ago. 3 m long, 1 m at the hip, about 25 kg. Carnivore. Hundreds were found buried together at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico; it is the state fossil of New Mexico.
Herrerasaurus. Pronounced: heh – rair – ah – sore – us. Herrerasaurus.
Herrerasaurus

Herrerasaurus. Late Triassic, 231 million years ago. 6 m long, 1.1 m at the hip, about 350 kg. Carnivore. One of the earliest known dinosaurs, from the Ischigualasto badlands of Argentina, with a sliding jaw joint for gripping prey.
Eoraptor. Pronounced: ee – oh – rap – tor. Eoraptor.
Eoraptor

Eoraptor. Late Triassic, 231 million years ago. 1 m long, 0.4 m at the hip, about 10 kg. Omnivore. The "dawn thief" is among the very first dinosaurs; its mixed teeth suggest it ate both plants and small animals.
Plateosaurus. Pronounced: plat – ee – oh – sore – us. Plateosaurus.
Plateosaurus

Plateosaurus. Late Triassic, 214–204 million years ago. 7 m long, 2 m at the hip, about 1 tonne. Herbivore. Europe's most common Triassic dinosaur; hundreds of skeletons come from Germany and Switzerland, many trapped in mud.
Riojasaurus. Pronounced: ree – oh – hah – sore – us. Riojasaurus.
Riojasaurus

Riojasaurus. Late Triassic, 227–208 million years ago. 10 m long, 2 m at the hip, about 3 tonnes. Herbivore. An early four-legged sauropodomorph from Argentina with unusually heavy limb bones for its time.
Staurikosaurus. Pronounced: store – ik – oh – sore – us. Staurikosaurus.
Staurikosaurus

Staurikosaurus. Late Triassic, 233 million years ago. 2 m long, 0.6 m at the hip, about 30 kg. Carnivore. Found in Brazil, it is one of the oldest dinosaurs known, a lightly built runner with a long tail.
Postosuchus. Pronounced: post – oh – soo – kus. Postosuchus.
Postosuchus

Postosuchus. Late Triassic, 228–202 million years ago. 4.5 m long, 1.2 m at the hip, about 250 kg. Carnivore. Not a dinosaur: a crocodile-line archosaur that was the top predator of Triassic North America, before dinosaurs took over.
Placerias. Pronounced: plah – seer – ee – us. Placerias.
Placerias

Placerias. Late Triassic, 221–210 million years ago. 3.5 m long, 1.5 m at the shoulder, about 1 tonne. Herbivore. A tusked dicynodont, a distant mammal relative rather than a dinosaur, and one of the last of its kind.
Nothosaurus. Pronounced: no – tho – sore – us. Nothosaurus.
Nothosaurus
Nothosaurus. Middle–Late Triassic, 240–210 million years ago. 4 m long, about 150 kg. Piscivore. A seal-like fish hunter that hauled out on shore; its paddle limbs still had separate fingers.
Shonisaurus. Pronounced: show – nee – sore – us. Shonisaurus.
Shonisaurus

Shonisaurus. Late Triassic, 215 million years ago. 15 m long, about 30 tonnes. Piscivore. Nevada's state fossil and, for decades, the largest marine reptile known; dozens lie together at Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park.
Eudimorphodon. Pronounced: you – dih – mor – fo – don. Eudimorphodon.
Eudimorphodon
Eudimorphodon. Late Triassic, 210 million years ago. 1 m wingspan long, about 10 kg. Piscivore. One of the earliest pterosaurs, with multi-pointed teeth suited to gripping slippery fish.
Tanystropheus. Pronounced: tan – ee – stro – fee – us. Tanystropheus.
Tanystropheus

Tanystropheus. Middle Triassic, 242–235 million years ago. 6 m long, about 100 kg. Piscivore. Its neck was longer than body and tail combined yet had only 13 vertebrae; it likely ambushed fish from the shallows.
Brachiosaurus. Pronounced: brack – ee – oh – sore – us. Brachiosaurus.
Brachiosaurus

Brachiosaurus. Late Jurassic, 154–150 million years ago. 22 m long, 12 m to the head, about 30–60 tonnes. Herbivore. The name means "arm lizard": its front legs were longer than its back legs, giving it a giraffe-like posture for browsing treetops.
Diplodocus. Pronounced: dih – plod – oh – kus. Diplodocus.
Diplodocus

Diplodocus. Late Jurassic, 154–152 million years ago. 26 m long, 4–5 m at the hip, about 12–15 tonnes. Herbivore. More than half its length was tail. One hypothesis holds the whip-like tip could be cracked faster than the speed of sound.
Apatosaurus. Pronounced: ah – pat – oh – sore – us. Apatosaurus.
Apatosaurus

Apatosaurus. Late Jurassic, 152–151 million years ago. 22 m long, 4.5 m at the hip, about 20 tonnes. Herbivore. Long confused with "Brontosaurus", it had an unusually thick, heavy neck and a whip-like tail.
Stegosaurus. Pronounced: steg – oh – sore – us. Stegosaurus.
Stegosaurus

Stegosaurus. Late Jurassic, 155–150 million years ago. 9 m long, 4 m to the plates, about 5 tonnes. Herbivore. Its brain was the size of a walnut; the tail spikes are nicknamed the "thagomizer" after a Far Side cartoon.
Allosaurus. Pronounced: al – oh – sore – us. Allosaurus.
Allosaurus

Allosaurus. Late Jurassic, 155–145 million years ago. 8.5 m long, 2.5 m at the hip, about 2.5 tonnes. Carnivore. Top predator of the Morrison Formation; it may have swung its hatchet-like upper jaw down into prey rather than biting.
Dilophosaurus. Pronounced: dy – loaf – oh – sore – us. Dilophosaurus.
Dilophosaurus

Dilophosaurus. Early Jurassic, 193 million years ago. 7 m long, 1.8 m at the hip, about 400 kg. Carnivore. The real animal had no neck frill and no venom; it did have two thin bony crests along its snout.
Kentrosaurus. Pronounced: ken – tro – sore – us. Kentrosaurus.
Kentrosaurus

Kentrosaurus. Late Jurassic, 152 million years ago. 4.5 m long, 1.5 m at the hip, about 1 tonne. Herbivore. A small East African stegosaur: plates over the shoulders give way to long paired spikes down the back and tail.
Mamenchisaurus. Pronounced: mah – men – chee – sore – us. Mamenchisaurus.
Mamenchisaurus

Mamenchisaurus. Late Jurassic, 160–145 million years ago. 25 m long, 3.5 m at the hip, about 15 tonnes. Herbivore. Its neck alone could reach 15 m, about half its total length, one of the longest necks of any animal.
Compsognathus. Pronounced: komp – sog – nah – thus. Compsognathus.
Compsognathus
Compsognathus. Late Jurassic, 150 million years ago. 1 m long, 0.3 m at the hip, about 3 kg. Carnivore. Chicken-sized; one specimen was fossilised with a whole lizard in its stomach.
Rhamphorhynchus. Pronounced: ram – fo – rink – us. Rhamphorhynchus.
Rhamphorhynchus

Rhamphorhynchus. Late Jurassic, 150 million years ago. 1.8 m wingspan long, about 1.5 kg. Piscivore. A long-tailed pterosaur with a diamond-shaped vane at the tip and needle teeth angled outward for snatching fish.
Plesiosaurus. Pronounced: plee – see – oh – sore – us. Plesiosaurus.
Plesiosaurus

Plesiosaurus. Early Jurassic, 199–175 million years ago. 3.5 m long, about 100 kg. Piscivore. Described in 1821 from Mary Anning's finds at Lyme Regis; it flew through the water with four wing-like flippers.
Ichthyosaurus. Pronounced: ik – thee – oh – sore – us. Ichthyosaurus.
Ichthyosaurus
Ichthyosaurus. Early Jurassic, 200–190 million years ago. 3 m long, about 90 kg. Piscivore. Dolphin-shaped but a reptile; fossils show it gave birth to live young at sea, tail first.
Liopleurodon. Pronounced: ly – oh – ploor – oh – don. Liopleurodon.
Liopleurodon

Liopleurodon. Middle–Late Jurassic, 165–155 million years ago. 6.5 m long, about 1.5 tonnes. Carnivore. A short-necked pliosaur with a crocodile-like skull; its nostrils may have let it smell underwater in stereo.
Tyrannosaurus rex. Pronounced: tie – ran – oh – sore – us rex. Tyrannosaurus rex.
Tyrannosaurus rex

Tyrannosaurus rex. Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago. 12 m long, 4 m at the hip, about 8 tonnes. Carnivore. Its bite was the strongest of any known land animal, and those famous little arms were still strong enough to lift more than a person.
Triceratops. Pronounced: try – sair – ah – tops. Triceratops.
Triceratops

Triceratops. Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago. 8–9 m long, 3 m at the shoulder, about 6–12 tonnes. Herbivore. It carried several hundred teeth packed into batteries that were replaced continually, shearing tough plants like scissors.
Velociraptor. Pronounced: veh – loss – ih – rap – tor. Velociraptor.
Velociraptor

Velociraptor. Late Cretaceous, 75–71 million years ago. 2 m long, 0.5 m at the hip, about 15 kg. Carnivore. Turkey-sized and feathered: fossils of its forearm bones show quill knobs, the same anchors that hold flight feathers in modern birds.
Spinosaurus. Pronounced: spy – no – sore – us. Spinosaurus.
Spinosaurus

Spinosaurus. Late Cretaceous, 99–93 million years ago. 14 m long, 2.8 m at the hip, about 7 tonnes. Piscivore. The largest known predatory dinosaur, with a 1.5 m sail and a crocodile-like snout; it probably hunted in rivers.
Ankylosaurus. Pronounced: ang – ky – lo – sore – us. Ankylosaurus.
Ankylosaurus

Ankylosaurus. Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago. 7 m long, 1.7 m, about 6 tonnes. Herbivore. A living tank: bony armor even covered its eyelids, and the tail club could have broken a tyrannosaur's leg.
Parasaurolophus. Pronounced: pair – ah – sore – ol – oh – fus. Parasaurolophus.
Parasaurolophus

Parasaurolophus. Late Cretaceous, 76–73 million years ago. 9.5 m long, 2.7 m at the hip, about 2.5 tonnes. Herbivore. The hollow crest was a resonating chamber; computer models suggest it produced a low, trombone-like call.
Iguanodon. Pronounced: ig – wan – oh – don. Iguanodon.
Iguanodon

Iguanodon. Early Cretaceous, 126–122 million years ago. 10 m long, 2.7 m at the hip, about 3.5 tonnes. Herbivore. The second dinosaur ever named; its thumb spike was at first mistaken for a nose horn.
Pachycephalosaurus. Pronounced: pak – ee – sef – ah – lo – sore – us. Pachycephalosaurus.
Pachycephalosaurus

Pachycephalosaurus. Late Cretaceous, 70–66 million years ago. 4.5 m long, 1.5 m at the hip, about 400 kg. Omnivore. Its skull dome was up to 25 cm thick; healed injuries on some domes suggest they really did butt heads.
Carnotaurus. Pronounced: kar – no – tore – us. Carnotaurus.
Carnotaurus

Carnotaurus. Late Cretaceous, 72–69 million years ago. 8 m long, 2.4 m at the hip, about 1.5 tonnes. Carnivore. The "meat-eating bull" had horns over its eyes and arms even smaller than T. rex's; it may have been the fastest large theropod.
Therizinosaurus. Pronounced: thair – ih – zeen – oh – sore – us. Therizinosaurus.
Therizinosaurus

Therizinosaurus. Late Cretaceous, 70 million years ago. 10 m long, 3 m at the hip, about 5 tonnes. Herbivore. A pot-bellied, plant-eating theropod whose hand claws reached a metre long, the longest of any animal.
Gallimimus. Pronounced: gal – ih – my – mus. Gallimimus.
Gallimimus
Gallimimus. Late Cretaceous, 70 million years ago. 6 m long, 1.9 m at the hip, about 440 kg. Omnivore. An ostrich-like runner, probably the fastest dinosaur of its size at 50 km/h or more.
Pteranodon. Pronounced: teh – ran – oh – don. Pteranodon.
Pteranodon

Pteranodon. Late Cretaceous, 86–84 million years ago. 6.5 m wingspan long, about 25 kg. Piscivore. Toothless and crested; over a thousand specimens are known from the chalk of Kansas, once a shallow inland sea.
Quetzalcoatlus. Pronounced: ket – sal – ko – at – lus. Quetzalcoatlus.
Quetzalcoatlus

Quetzalcoatlus. Late Cretaceous, 68 million years ago. 10.5 m wingspan long, 5 m standing, about 250 kg. Carnivore. The largest flying animal ever: as tall as a giraffe on the ground, with the wingspan of a small aeroplane.
Mosasaurus. Pronounced: moe – zah – sore – us. Mosasaurus.
Mosasaurus

Mosasaurus. Late Cretaceous, 82–66 million years ago. 15 m long, about 14 tonnes. Carnivore. A giant sea lizard related to monitors and snakes, with a second set of teeth in the roof of its mouth to ratchet prey down.
Elasmosaurus. Pronounced: eh – lazz – mo – sore – us. Elasmosaurus.
Elasmosaurus
Elasmosaurus. Late Cretaceous, 80 million years ago. 12 m long, about 2 tonnes. Piscivore. Its 7 m neck held 72 vertebrae; the first describer famously mounted the skull on the wrong end.

clips.text: Exhibit 1. The king on Broadway. Twelve metres of Tyrannosaurus against the billboards. Cabs swerve; nobody films in landscape.
Exhibit 2. Taller than the arches. Brachiosaurus browses at twelve metres. It walks straight under the tower without ducking.
Exhibit 3. Something in the Thames. A fifteen-metre sea lizard beneath Tower Bridge. The bascules will not be raised.
Exhibit 4. Wings over the harbour. The largest flying animal ever, ten metres across, circling the Opera House at dusk.
Exhibit 5. Among the penguins. Turkey-sized, feathered, and much faster than anything else on the ice shelf.
Exhibit 6. The longest tail on the ridge. Twenty-six metres of Diplodocus on a walkway built for two people abreast.
